interactive.whatAmILookingAt: The picture runs over fourteen small screens. The main picture is a disc on a shaft, seen end on. The disc has a heavy spot on it. The disc and shaft weigh 50 kg in all. The heavy spot is an example 20 g. It sits 0.15 m from the axis. The figure labels the 20 g spot, the 50 kg disc and shaft and the 500 kN/m mounts. The shaft's bearing sits on springy mounts that let it move up and down. Together the mounts are 500 kN/m stiff. An arrow from the axis to the heavy spot shows the spot's outward pull on the shaft. It turns with the disc and grows as you speed up. The speed drag runs from 0 to 2400 rev/min in 5 rev/min steps. It opens at 300 rev/min. As you sweep, each speed leaves a dot on a graph of shake against speed. So the response curve builds as you go. A damping slider runs the damping factor from 0.02 to 0.30 in steps of 0.01. It opens at an example 0.05. The rule for the pull is this. A mass going round a circle needs a pull towards the centre. That pull is m r ω²: its mass × its radius × the angular speed squared. The speed is in rad/s. So the spot pulls the shaft outwards just as hard. 300 rev/min is 31.4 rad/s. There the pull is 0.02 × 0.15 × 31.4² = 3.0 N. At 1450 rev/min the pull is 69 N. That speed is 151.8 rad/s. Seen from the side, the turning pull pushes the mounts up, then down, once a turn. The rule for the mounts is this. A mass M on a stiffness k swings on its own at its natural frequency, √(k ÷ M). Here that is √(500,000 ÷ 50) = 100 rad/s, or 100 ÷ 2π = 15.9 times a second. So the critical speed is 15.9 turns a second. That is 955 rev/min. The shake is the steady swing of a driven spring and mass: shake = m r ω² ÷ √((k − M ω²)² + (c ω)²). Here c is the damping. It is 2 × the damping factor × √(k M). At the critical speed this comes to m r ÷ M ÷ (2 × the damping factor). The heavy spot moves the rotor's centre of mass off the shaft's line. The offset is m r ÷ M = 0.003 ÷ 50 m, which is 0.06 mm. Far above the critical speed, the rotor turns about that centre of mass. So the shake settles near 0.06 mm. At damping 0.05 the shake is 0.007 mm at 300 rev/min, 0.6 mm at 955 rev/min, 0.11 mm at 1450 rev/min and 0.07 mm at 2400 rev/min. At damping 0.2 the peak is wider and about 0.15 mm high. It sits near 995 rev/min. At 0.02 it is 1.5 mm. A balance weight of 20 g also sits 0.15 m out. You can drag it round the rim in 15° steps. It opens a quarter turn from the heavy spot. Its pull is an arrow too. The two arrows add, as forces do. Beside the spot, the total pull is twice as big. A quarter turn away, it is 1.41 times as big. Opposite the spot, the two pulls cancel at every speed. The arrows vanish and the curve goes flat at zero. Readouts give the heavy spot's pull in N, the shake in mm and the shaft speed in rad/s. The shake is the amplitude, each way from rest. A bracket beside the mounts, labelled ± shake, spans it both ways. On a narrow phone the three readouts wrap onto two lines. The disc turns 20 times slower than real. The readouts give real speeds. The shake is drawn 40 times bigger than real. A caption says so on the four rotor screens only. Screen 1 has a mass on a spring with a natural frequency of 2 Hz. The mass bobs gently at its own 2 Hz. A push that comes and goes drives it. The screen asks which push gives the biggest steady swing. The right pick is a push at 2 Hz. The wrong picks are the slowest push at 0.5 Hz and the fastest push at 8 Hz. Screen 2 drags the speed from 300 to 1450 rev/min. The pull arrow grows from 3.0 N to 69 N and turns with the spot. The mounts are held still here, and the shake readout is hidden. A second arrow at the mounts shows the pull's up-and-down part. It pushes them up, then down, once a turn. Screen 3 gives the pull as 69 N at 1450 rev/min. It asks the pull at 2900 rev/min. The answer is 277 N, four times as big. The speed doubles, and speed counts twice. The wrong pick 138 N doubles the pull with the speed. The wrong pick 69 N treats speed as making no difference. Screen 4 shows the natural frequency worked out: √(500,000 ÷ 50) = 100 rad/s, and 100 ÷ 2π = 15.9 times a second. It works out the 0.06 mm offset as 0.003 kg m ÷ 50 kg. It sweeps the speed from 0 to 2400 rev/min at damping 0.05. The curve builds dot by dot. The shake is tiny at first. It peaks at about 0.6 mm near 955 rev/min. Then it falls back to 0.11 mm at 1450 rev/min and settles near 0.06 mm. Screen 5 has a pump set whose mounts swing on their own at 20 Hz. It asks where the pump shakes hardest on its way up to 2900 rev/min. The answer is 1200 rev/min, from 20 × 60. The wrong pick 2900 rev/min is its top speed, as if shaking just grew with speed. The wrong pick 20 rev/min forgets to turn the hertz into rev/min. Screen 6 says a damping factor of 1 is critical damping, so 0.05 is light. It says why the peak is 0.06 mm ÷ (2 × the damping factor): at the critical speed the spring and the rotor's inertia cancel, so only damping holds back the pull. It drags the damping slider from 0.05 to 0.2. The peak drops from 0.6 mm to about 0.15 mm and spreads wider. Away from the peak, the shake hardly changes. At 0.02 the peak climbs to 1.5 mm. Screen 7 doubles the damping factor from 0.05 to 0.1. It asks the shake at the critical speed. The answer is 0.3 mm, half of 0.6 mm. The wrong pick 0 mm treats damping as removing the shake. The wrong pick 0.6 mm treats damping as only moving the peak. Screen 8 drags the balance weight round the rim from a quarter turn away. Beside the spot the pull doubles. Opposite it, the pulls cancel and the curve goes flat at every speed. Screen 9 has a 30 g heavy spot 0.10 m from the axis. The balance weight goes opposite, 0.15 m out. The screen asks the weight's mass. The answer is 20 g: 30 g × 0.10 m = 3 g m, and 3 g m ÷ 0.15 m = 20 g. The wrong pick 30 g copies the spot's mass. The wrong pick 45 g turns the radii upside down. Screen 10 turns on Long rotor. It shows a long rotor from the side. A 20 g heavy spot sits near each end, on opposite sides. The two pulls cancel in total. Yet together they rock the shaft end over end, as a couple. A balance weight at each end, opposite each spot, stops the rocking. Screens 11 to 13 mix it all. Screen 11 has a motor running up to 1450 rev/min. It shakes hard for a moment near 950 rev/min, then runs smoothly. The screen asks why. The right pick is that it passes through a critical speed. One wrong pick says the heavy spot pulls hardest at 950 rev/min. The other says the motor is short of torque at 950 rev/min. Screen 12 asks the pull of a 10 g heavy spot 0.2 m out at 3000 rev/min. That speed is 314.2 rad/s. So the pull is 0.01 × 0.2 × 314.2² = 197 N. The wrong pick 18,000 N leaves the speed in rev/min. The wrong pick 5 N uses 50 rev/s. Screen 13 stiffens the 50 kg rotor's mounts from 500 to 2000 kN/m. It asks the new critical speed. The answer is 1910 rev/min, because four times the stiffness doubles √(k ÷ M). The Why? adds that more mass would lower it. The wrong pick 3820 rev/min is four times as fast. The wrong pick 477 rev/min treats stiffer mounts as lowering it. Screen 14 is a still panel of what comes next. Bending in beams and the twist in a shaft carrying torque build on moments and stress. The shaft's two torques wrap round its axis, turning opposite ways at its two ends. Screen 14 has no Play again. Some screens show an idea and the rest ask you to try it. Each puzzle offers three answers. A wrong pick is drawn so you can see where it goes wrong.
interactive.ignores: The mounts let the rotor move only up and down. They are drawn as simple springs. Real mounts let it move every way. The shaft itself bends a little too. That gives a real machine more than one critical speed. The damping is a setting, not worked out from the mounts' material. The heavy spot is drawn far bigger than a real one. The disc turns 20 times slower than real. The shake is drawn 40 times bigger. The curve shows the steady shake at each speed. On a real run-up the shake takes a moment to build. So a quick pass through the critical speed shakes less than the curve shows. The long rotor's view is a sketch. It does not compute the size of the rocking.

explain.text:
A heavy spot on a spinning rotor pulls its shaft outwards. The pull turns with it. So it pushes the mounts one way, then the other, once every turn. The shaking is worst near one speed. There the turning rate matches the rate the mounts swing at on their own. A balance weight opposite the heavy spot cancels that pull at every speed. It needs the same mass × radius.

Start with the pull. A mass going round a circle needs a pull towards the centre to stay on it. That pull is m r ω²: the mass × its radius × the angular speed squared. The speed is in rad/s. A rotor with more mass on one side of its axis than the other has an [[unbalance]]. Its shaft must pull that heavy spot inwards. By Newton's third law, the spot pulls the shaft outwards just as hard. That outward pull points at the spot wherever it is, so it turns with the shaft. The speed counts twice. At double the speed, the spot moves twice as fast and swings its direction round twice as quickly. So the pull is four times as big. Take a 20 g spot 0.15 m from the axis at 1450 rev/min. That speed is 151.8 rad/s. Its pull is 0.02 × 0.15 × 151.8² = 69 N. At 2900 rev/min it is 277 N.

Now the mounts. Remember the driven swing. A mass M on a spring of stiffness k swings on its own at its natural frequency. That is √(k ÷ M) in rad/s. Stiffer mounts raise it. A heavier rotor lowers it. Here the mass is a 50 kg rotor on mounts 500 kN/m stiff. They swing on their own at √(500,000 ÷ 50) = 100 rad/s. That is 100 ÷ 2π = 15.9 times a second. Seen from the side, the turning pull is a push that comes and goes once a turn. At 15.9 turns a second, each push arrives in step with the swing and adds to it. That speed is 955 rev/min. It is the rotor's [[critical speed]].[^1] Well below it, the pull is small and the stiff mounts give only a little. Well above it, each push reverses before the rotor's 50 kg can get moving. So the rotor cannot follow. It turns about its own centre of mass instead. The heavy spot moves that centre off the shaft's line by m r ÷ M. That is 0.003 kg m ÷ 50 kg = 0.00006 m, or 0.06 mm. So the shake falls back from its peak and settles near 0.06 mm. The shaking does not just grow with speed. It peaks, then falls.

Damping takes energy out of every swing. More damping gives a lower, wider peak. The damping factor says how much. At 1 it is critical damping, where a nudged mass settles without swinging. So 0.05 is light. At the critical speed the spring and the rotor's inertia cancel each other. Only damping holds back the turning pull. So the peak is 0.06 mm ÷ (2 × the damping factor). At a damping factor of 0.05 that is 0.6 mm. A running speed near there would shake hard. So machines are run clear of their critical speeds. Doubling the damping halves the peak.

Damping softens the peak, but the pull is still there. Balancing removes it. Fit a balance weight with the same mass × radius on the opposite side. Its pull is just as big and points the other way, at every speed. The two pulls cancel. In the model nothing is left to drive the mounts. A real balance leaves a small remainder. A long rotor needs more care. Put a heavy spot near each end, on opposite sides. The two cancel in total but still rock the shaft end over end, as a couple. A rigid rotor is balanced with weights at its two ends. A flexible one needs weights in more places. This is a simplified model. A real rotor moves every way on its mounts, and its shaft bends. Each way it can move is a [[normal mode]], like the two masses on springs you met in linear algebra. Each mode has its own natural frequency. So a real rotor has more than one critical speed.

Vibration also tells you how a machine is doing. Unbalance is one cause. Misalignment, looseness, worn rolling bearings and gear wear show up too. After unbalance, misalignment is the commonest cause. A spectrum shows how much shake there is at each frequency. Its pattern tells bearing wear, misalignment and electrical causes apart. **An unbalanced rotor shakes its mounts hardest near its critical speed, where its turning rate matches the mounts' natural frequency.**

analogy.text: Think of a series RLC circuit on a supply whose frequency you can turn up. Its current peaks at the resonant frequency. Resistance lowers and widens that peak, as damping does here. Now picture a supply whose voltage grows with the frequency squared. That is the heavy spot's pull. Balancing is like disconnecting the supply. No amount of resistance does that.
analogy.breaks: Even with that growing supply, the circuit's current keeps rising above resonance. The rotor's shake settles at a steady size instead. The shake behaves like the capacitor's charge, not the current. A rotor also shakes in space, in more than one direction. A circuit has nothing like that.

practice.text:
- Safe way first: isolate and lock off the machine. Wait until the rotor has stopped and cannot windmill before you touch it or fit a balance weight. A balance weight's fixing must hold its pull of m r ω², which is large at speed. So fix it firmly, refit the guards and stand clear for a run.
- Note the speed where the shaking peaks on a run-up or run-down. That is near a critical speed.
- Compare it with the running speed. Machines are designed to run at speeds away from their critical speeds. For a shaft's twisting vibration, aim to keep the running speed at least 10% clear of a critical speed where you can.[^2] No fixed margin is given here for side-to-side critical speeds like this rotor's.
- Critical speed in rev/min = the natural frequency in Hz × 60.
- Work out an unbalance pull as m r ω², with ω in rad/s: rev/min × 2π ÷ 60.
- To balance a single disc, fit a weight opposite the heavy spot with the same mass × radius. Balance mass = the spot's mass × its radius ÷ the weight's radius.
- Balance a long, stiff rotor at both ends. A flexible one needs more places.
- The shake here is measured each way from rest. Vibration is often quoted peak to peak, which is twice that.
- Use vibration to find faults. It shows unbalance, misalignment, looseness, worn rolling bearings and gear wear. If shaking remains after balancing, check the coupling's alignment next. A frequency spectrum tells the causes apart.
- ISO 20816-1 sets out how to measure and judge machine vibration.[^3]

**Rules of thumb:** double the speed and an unbalance pulls four times as hard. Damping softens a resonance. Balancing removes the unbalance that drives it.

**Worked example:** a fan has a 12 g heavy spot 0.25 m from its axis and runs at 1480 rev/min. That is 1480 × 2π ÷ 60 = 155.0 rad/s. The pull is 0.012 × 0.25 × 155.0² = 72.1 N, turning with the fan. A balance weight goes 0.2 m out, opposite the spot. Its mass is 12 × 0.25 ÷ 0.2 = 15 g.

**Common mistakes**
- Leaving the speed in rev/min in m r ω².
- Expecting the shake to rise with speed for ever. It peaks near the critical speed and falls back above it.
- Adding damping to cure an unbalance. It softens the peak, but the pull remains.
- Matching the balance weight's mass, not its mass × radius.
- Fitting the balance weight on the same side as the heavy spot.

checks.label: Unbalance forces are proportional to the rotating speed of the rotor squared: at every speed, twice the speed gives four times the pull
The pull is the mass × the radius × the angular speed squared, in rad/s: 31.4 rad/s and 3 N at 300 rev/min, 151.8 rad/s and 69 N at 1450, and 277 N at 2900, where doubling once would give 138
Dynamic resonance: the rotor speed at which the shake peaks is the critical speed, where the shaft turns as often as the mounts swing on their own
The mounts swing on their own at √(500,000 ÷ 50) = 100 rad/s, 15.9 times a second, so the critical speed is 955 rev/min, where the shake is 0.06 mm ÷ (2 × 0.05) = 0.6 mm
At damping 0.05 the shake is 0.007 mm at 300 rev/min, 0.11 mm at 1450 and 0.07 mm at 2400, and far above the critical speed it settles towards the 0.06 mm offset of the centre of mass
The greatest response is for the least amount of damping: across the damping slider, less damping always gives a higher peak
More damping gives a lower, wider peak: 1.5 mm at 0.02, 0.6 mm at 0.05, and 0.15 mm near 995 rev/min at 0.2, while at 300 and 2400 rev/min the shake hardly changes
Resonance occurs when the driving frequency equals the natural frequency: of the three pushes on the mass on a spring, the one at its own frequency swings it most
A balance weight with the same mass × radius cancels the pull at every speed opposite the spot, doubles it beside the spot, and makes it 1.41 times a quarter turn away
A rigid rotor can be balanced at the two end planes: a weight at each end, opposite each spot, leaves no pull at either end, while without them the pulls cancel in total but rock the shaft
Every puzzle answer is worked from its rule: 2 Hz, 277 N, 1200 rev/min, 0.3 mm, 20 g, 197 N and 1910 rev/min, with the wrong picks 138, 2900, 20, 0, 0.6, 30, 45, 18,000, 5, 3820 and 477
Each puzzle offers three answers and accepts only its right one; every wrong answer has its own hint and its working drawn in red, and nothing is marked before Check
Every demonstration ends within 5 s of its screen opening, and every answer is drawn within 2.5 s of Check
Every screen that shows an idea says it in 90 words or fewer

steps: A shake on the way up

applied.problem: "Worst at one speed" and "hardest at its critical speed" are too exact: with damping the peak sits a little above it (the model's own 0.2 damping peaks near 995 rev/min, not 955). And "the slow shaft is made thick" is absolute, out of i7's context.

Isolating does not stop a coasting rotor or a fan windmilling in a draught, and a trial run with fitted weights needs guards on and people clear. "Balance a long rotor at both ends" contradicts the explanation: a flexible rotor needs more planes. "Removes its cause" overstates it.

The analogy maps shake to current, but with a supply growing as frequency squared the current keeps rising above resonance; the shake's true match is the capacitor's charge, which settles as the shake does.
